region.en: Seneca hunting country, western New York
region.zh: 紐約州西部塞內卡獵場

texts.period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (BAE Ann. Rep. 2, 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Hi-nun destroying the giant animals'

summary.en: Caught in a thunder-shower, a hunter hears a voice calling him upward into the clouds, where thunder-beings tell him to look for a huge water-serpent below. His eyes anointed, he sees the monster; when a Thunderer fails, the hunter draws his bow and kills it - man's first acquaintance with Hi-nun and proof that the Thunder God protects the human race from dragons and serpents.
summary.zh: 獵人遭雷雨所困，聞聲召其昇入雲端，雷族之人命他俯視尋找巨水蛇。經長老以膏抹其眼，他得見怪物；當雷者失利時，獵人張弓射殺之——此乃人類初識雷神希農，亦證雷神護佑人類、誅除龍蛇。

sensitivity.note: Erminnie Smith fieldwork with Cayuga and Seneca informants, 1878-1881 (published 1883); public domain. Tobacco offering to thunder remains a living practice; described here as belief.

passages.text: A hunter in the woods was once caught in a thunder-shower, when he heard a voice calling upon him to follow. This he did until he found himself in the clouds, the height of many trees from the ground. Beings which seemed to be men surrounded him, with one among them who seemed to be their chief. He was told to look below and tell whether he could see a huge water-serpent. Replying that he could not, the old man anointed his eyes, after which he could see the monster in the depths below him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: They then ordered one of their number to try and kill this enemy to the human race. Upon his failing, the hunter was told to accomplish the feat. He accordingly drew his bow and killed the foe. He was then conducted back to the place where he had sought shelter from the storm, which had now ceased. This was man's first acquaintance with the Thunder God and his assistants, and by it he learned that they were friendly toward the human race, and protected it from dragons, serpents, and other enemies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Hi-nun and Niagara: How the Horseshoe Falls Were Fashioned
title.zh: 希農與尼亞加拉：馬蹄瀑之形成

region.zh: 尼亞加拉瀑布，紐約與安大略交界

texts.period: Recorded 1878-1881 by Erminnie A. Smith (1883), 'A Seneca legend'

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'A Seneca legend of Hi-nun and Niagara'

summary.en: A maiden about to be forced to marry a hideous old suitor launches her canoe on the roaring Niagara. Hi-nun, the God of Cloud and Rain, who dwells in a cave behind the falls, catches her as her bark dashes on the rocks; in his cave she learns that a snake coiled beneath the village poisons the springs because it craves human flesh. Sent home, she moves the tribe nearer the lake; the serpent drags itself after them, and Hi-nun slays it with thunderbolts. The vast corpse, wedged between the rocks, rises the waters mountains high until the rocks give way - thus the horseshoe form was fashioned - and the Indians had no more fever.
summary.zh: 少女被迫嫁給醜陋老者，遂駕獨木舟衝入尼亞加拉的怒濤。居於瀑後岩洞的雲雨之神希農，在她的小舟撞上岩石之際展翅將其救起；她在洞中得知村下盤蛇毒化泉水的緣由——蛇嗜人肉。她返鄉說服族人遷近湖畔；蛇卻緩緩追至，希農以雷霆誅之。巨蛇屍身被岩隙夾住，水位暴漲如山，岩石崩裂——馬蹄之形由此而成——村中疫病遂止。

sensitivity.note: Seneca legend (Smith 1883); public domain. A place-myth for the Horseshoe Falls themselves.

passages.text: A beautiful Indian maiden was about to be compelled by her family to marry a hideous old Indian. Despair was in her heart; she knew there was no escape for her, so in desperation she leaped into her canoe and pushed it from shore on the roaring waters of Niagara, heeding not that she was going to her death, preferring the angry waters to the arms of her detested lover. Now, the God of Cloud and Rain, the great deity Hi-nun, who watches over the harvest, dwelt in a cave behind the rushing waters. He spread out his wings and flew to her rescue, and caught her just as her frail bark was dashing on the rocks below.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: The grateful Indian girl lived for many weeks in Hi-nun's cave. She learned from him why her people died so often - why sickness was always busy among them. He told her how a snake lay coiled up under the ground beneath the village, and how he crept out and poisoned the springs, because he lived upon human beings and craved their flesh more and more. Hi-nun kept the maiden till he learned the ugly old suitor was dead; then he bade her return and tell her tribe what she had learned. She taught them all he had told her and begged them to break up their settlement and travel nearer to the lake; and her words prevailed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: For a while sickness ceased, but it broke out again, for the serpent was far too cunning to be so easily outwitted: he dragged himself slowly but surely after the people. Hi-nun watched him until he neared the creek, then launched a thunderbolt at him - then another, and another, before finally the poisoner was slain. The great dead snake stretched over more than twenty arrow flights, and as he floated down the waters of Niagara it was as if a mountain appeared above them. His corpse was too large to pass the rocks, so it became wedged in between them, and the waters rose over it mountains high. As the weight of the monster pressed on the rocks they gave way, and thus the horseshoe form, that remains to this day, was fashioned. But the Indians had no more fever in their settlement.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Thunderers: The Castaway, the Old Man, and the Great Grub
title.zh: 雷族：被棄者、老者與巨蠹

region.en: Mountain pit and cornfields of the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的山穴與玉米田

texts.period: Related by Horatio Hale from an Indian chief; recorded by Smith (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The Thunderers'

summary.en: Comrades carrying a crippled warrior hurl him into a mountain pit to die; an old gray-headed man heals him on condition he hunts for him. In spring the young man kills an enormous bear and is met by three figures in cloud-like garments - the Thunderers - who reveal the old man's true form, an enormous porcupine, and strike it dead with a bolt. Given a winged cloud-dress, the youth flies with them each spring; drinking from a pool, his shining lips betray the hiding place of the great patron grub that destroys corn and beans, which the Thunderers blast dry. Thence originated the honor in which the Thunder is held: many Iroquois still call Hi-nun their grandfather.
summary.zh: 同袍抬送折腿戰士途中，將其拋入山穴棄死；一位白髮老者治癒他，條件是為其狩獵。春季少年獵得巨熊，遇見三位身披雲衣者——雷族——他們揭示老者真身為巨豪豬，以雷殛之。少年獲贈帶翼雲袍，每年春天與雷族同飛；因池水潤唇而發亮，洩露了毀害玉米豆菽的巨蠹之首的藏身水池，雷族將其轟乾。雷神之尊崇由此而起——許多易洛魁人至今仍稱希農為祖父。

sensitivity.note: Hale's chief-informant text (Smith 1883); public domain. The Thunderers' mandate - rain, pest control, destruction of noxious things - is the charter of the Iroquois thunder-ritual.

passages.text: Three warriors on a distant expedition: one broke his leg, and by Indian law the others must carry him home. On a ridge of mountains they withdrew a little distance and took evil counsel together; returning to the litter they carried their helpless load near the brink of a deep pit in the mountain and suddenly hurled him in, then set off for their own country, reporting that he had died of wounds received in fight. They little imagined that he was still alive. When he recovered his senses he observed an old gray-headed man seated near him, crouching into a cavity on one side of the pit: 'You shall not die if you will promise to do what I require of you in return for saving you.' The young warrior promised to hunt for him, and the old man applied herbs to his wound and attended him skillfully until he recovered.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: One day he encountered an enormous bear, which he was lucky enough to kill, and heard a murmur of voices behind him: three men, or figures in the shape of men, clad in strange cloud-like garments, stood near. They informed him they were the Thunderers (Hi-nun), whose mission was to keep the earth and everything upon it in good order for the benefit of the human race - to bring rain in drought, to destroy serpents and other noxious creatures. Their present object was to destroy the old man to whom he had bound himself, who was a very different sort of being from what he pretended to be. They asked his aid, promising to convey him home to his mother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: He told the old man he had killed a bear and needed help to bring it home. The old man came out of the hollow, bade the youth examine the sky for the smallest speck of cloud, and followed him, looking upward with great anxiety. A cloud appeared and the thunder rumbled; the old man threw down his load and started to run, assuming his proper form of an enormous porcupine, which fled through the bushes discharging its quills like arrows backward as it ran. But the thunder followed, burst upon burst, until a bolt struck the huge animal, which fell lifeless into its den. The Thunderers then gave the young man a cloud-like robe with wings on its shoulders, rose with him into the air, and set him down in his mother's cornfield by night, where the widow, thinking she saw her son's ghost, was overjoyed: 'Do not be alarmed, mother; it is your son come back to take care of you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Every spring he put on the cloud-dress and flew with the Thunderers to witness what they did for the good of man. Passing above a mountain he became thirsty, descended to a pool to drink, and when he rejoined his companions his lips shone as if smeared with oil. 'Where have you been drinking?' 'In yonder pool.' 'There is something in that pool which we must destroy. We have sought it for years, and now you have happily found it for us.' They cast a mighty thunderbolt into the pool, which presently became dry; at the bottom, blasted by the thunder, was an immense grub - 'as big as a house,' said the chief - the special patron and representative of all grubs which destroy the corn and beans. Thence originated the honor in which the Thunder is held among the Indians. Many Iroquois still call Hi-nun their grandfather.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Echo God, Mars of the Iroquois

region.en: Hill country of the Six Nations, New York
region.zh: 紐約州六族之地的丘陵

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Echo God'

summary.en: In war the Echo God repeated only Iroquois war-cries through the hills, insuring victory and carrying home the evening recall; 'Goh-weh!' for each enemy slain, 'Oh-weh!' - our own - for a lost tribesman. If he answered not, a service was held to ask the cause of his anger; after a victorious war a dance was held to him, first mourning the dead. Since wars are over, the feast and dance to the Echo God have ceased.
summary.zh: 戰時，回聲神只在群山中重複易洛魁的戰呼，確保勝利，並於傍晚召回外出征戰者；每殺一敵呼「Goh-weh!」，折損族人則呼「Oh-weh!」——我族之人。若神不應，則行儀式問其怒因；戰勝後為他舉行舞蹈，先悼亡者。戰事既止，回聲神之祭舞遂不復行。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. War-practice deity of record; no operative war-magic is described.

passages.text: When engaged in wars with different nations the voice of the Echo God served for signals, as it would only respond to the calls of Iroquois. At the coming of evening it was used by them to call in those who were out on the war-path. When the warrior would whoop the Echo God would take it up and carry it on through the air, the enemy not being able to hear it, as this was the special god of the Six Nations. When enemies were killed their victors called out as many times as there were persons killed, the cry being 'Goh-weh! Goh-weh!' - 'I'm telling you!' But if one of their own tribe was killed they called out 'Oh-weh! Oh-weh!' meaning 'Our own!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: If no response was made by the Echo God it was an omen that they should not start; they continued calling, and if the god still remained silent, a service was held to ask the cause of his anger. When a warfare was ended victoriously a dance was held to the Echo God and the nations assembled to rejoice - but first to mourn for the dead and decide on the fate of the captives. As the Echo God was never called upon except in emergencies during warfare, now since wars are over the feast and dance to the Echo God have ceased to be a part of the Iroquois ceremonies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Extermination of the Stone Giants in the Great Gulf

region.en: Great gulf in the Seneca country (traditional)
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的巨壑（傳統）

texts.period: Related by O'Beille Beille, grandson of Cornplanter (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Extermination of the Stone Giants'

summary.en: The stone giants of the far West resolve to come east and exterminate the Indians; a Seneca war party is warned to accept the challenge and appoint a time and place. At the appointed hour, near a great gulf, a mighty wind from the west precipitates the whole race of giants into the abyss, from which they never extricate themselves - and the God of the West Wind is ever after held in reverence by the Senecas.
summary.zh: 遠在西部的石巨人決意東來誅滅印第安人；塞內卡戰隊受警，應下戰書，約定時地。屆時在巨壑之畔，西來的狂風將整個巨人種族吹墮深淵，永不得出——西風之神自此為塞內卡人所尊崇。

passages.text: The stone giants, who principally inhabited the far West, resolved to come East and exterminate the Indians. A party of Senecas, just starting out on the war-path, were warned of their impending danger and were bidden to accept the challenge to fight the stone giants and appoint a time and place. This they did. At the appointed time the giants appeared at the place, which was near a great gulf. Then there came a mighty wind from the west which precipitated the whole race of giants down into the abyss, from which they were never able to extricate themselves, and the God of the West Wind was ever after held in reverence by the Senecas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The North Wind, Ka-tash-huaht, the Icy Sacrifice-Demander
title.zh: 北風卡塔修特：索人為祭的冰魔

region.en: The frozen north (symbolic pin on the Canadian Shield, north of Lake Ontario)
region.zh: 冰封的北方（象徵性定位於安大略湖以北的加拿大地盾）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The North Wind'

summary.en: While medicine men go their customary rounds demanding gifts, an icy figure appears demanding a man as sacrifice. The Thunder God is appealed to and comes to the rescue with his assistants, chasing the figure far into the north, where the icy demon is doomed to remain: his howling and blustering are heard to this day, and his frosty children punish any venturesome mortal who intrudes too far toward his abode. He is termed Ka-tash-huaht, or North Wind, and ranks as an evil spirit.
summary.zh: 醫人循例向民眾收取獻禮之際，一個冰身之影出現，索一人為祭。眾人求助於雷神，雷神偕其助手追趕冰影遠入北方，將冰魔永逐於彼。至今猶聞其呼嘯怒號；凡人若敢深入其居所，他的霜之子嗣便會懲罰冒犯者。其名為卡塔修特，即北風，位列惡靈。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Companion piece to Parker's 'Coming of Spring.'

passages.text: It was the custom at a certain season for the medicine men to go about demanding gifts of the people; but an icy figure had also appeared, demanding a man as a sacrifice; whereupon the Thunder God was appealed to, and he came to the rescue with his assistants and chased the figure far into the north, where they doomed the icy demon to remain. To this day his howling and blustering are heard, and when any venturesome mortal dares to intrude too far towards his abode his frosty children soon punish the offender. He is termed Ka-tash-huaht, or North Wind, and ranks as an evil spirit.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Great Head: The Witch of the Continual Song and the Nine Brothers Raised
title.zh: 巨首：不停歌詠的巫婦與九兄弟復生

region.en: Rifted promontory in the distant wilderness (symbolic pin in the Adirondacks)
region.zh: 遠方荒野中的裂岩岬（象徵性定位於阿迪朗達克山）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Great Head'

summary.en: Great Head, a terrific human head with great eyes and streaming hair, growls 'I see thee, I see thee, thou shalt die' from his rifted rock. Nine brothers vanish one by one hunting; a mould-covered stranger dug from the earth turns out to be Great Head's own brother and entices him home with blocks of maple (his food); sent by the mole's cover, the youngest shoots the Head and mallets him at the door until he laughs, 'Si-h, si-h.' Great Head leads the youth to the witch who sings continually, whose word Schis-t-ki-an turns all to dry bones; they strip and burn her, set her year-old bones in rows, and at the hurricane's call the nine brothers rise shouting for joy.
summary.zh: 巨首——眼大髮長的可怕人首——自裂岩怒吼：「我看見你了，我看見你了，你必死。」九位兄長逐一獵行失蹤；自土中掘出的覆黴怪人原是巨首的親弟，以楓木塊（其食）誘其來家；最幼的兄弟借鼴鼠掩蔽射中巨首，又在門前以槌擊之，直至巨首笑出「Si-h, si-h」。巨首引少年往見不停歌詠的巫婦——其咒語「Schis-t-ki-an」使萬物化為枯骨。二人剝其皮、焚其身，將一年的骸骨排成行列；颶風一喚，九兄弟復生，相見歡呼。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Links the flying-head cycle to the witch-song motif; compare the quilt-of-eyes resurrection.

passages.text: It was a common belief among Indians that there was a strange, human-like creature, consisting simply of a head made terrific with large eyes and covered with long hair. His home was upon a huge rock, a rifted promontory, over which his long hair streamed in shaggy fierceness. Seen or unseen, if he saw anything that had the breath of life he growled: 'Kunn''-kun, Kunn''-kuin, wa''-h-tci'-ha''-i-h'; that is, 'I see thee, I see thee, thou shalt die,' or 'thou shalt suffer.' In a distant wilderness a man and his wife had ten children, all boys; the father died, and soon the mother, leaving the boys alone with their uncle. One by one the older brothers went hunting and did not return, until only the youngest brother and the aged uncle were left.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Stepping over a log the youngest heard a groan from the earth; digging, they found a man covered with mould, whom they revived with bear's oil. The stranger proved somewhat supernatural, and one night said, 'I cannot sleep; hearken to the great noise - it is my brother, the Great Head, howling through this hurricane. He is an awful being, for he destroys those who go near him... but perhaps I might entice him to come here. You must cut a huge maple tree into blocks, for that is what he eats.' Guided to the haunt and warned of the 'Great Eyes,' the young man called a mole: 'I want you to creep down under the grass where you will not be seen.' Hidden in the mole, he saw the Great Head watching an owl, drew his bow and shot an arrow into the Great Head, crying, 'I came after you.' The arrow became very large as it flew and small again as it returned.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: The Great Head came riding on a tempest to the very spot, and the hunter's arrow drove him away; these maneuvers were repeated many times. Meanwhile the uncle had prepared a mallet: as the Great Head came bursting through the door, the two men plied their mallets - at which the Great Head began to laugh, 'Si-h, si-h, si-h,' pleased to see his brother. When the tumult subsided the uncle gave him the maple blocks to eat. Then the Great Head said, 'I know where they have gone; they have gone to a place where lives a woman who is a witch and who sings continually... if he wishes to go to see this witch, I will show him her abode and all the bones of his brothers.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: They came to a place where they heard the witch singing; at length she spoke the word 'Schis-t-ki-an,' at which all turned to dry bones. The Great Head said, 'I will ask the question, How long have you been here? and the hair will fall from my head and you must replace it... then I will bite her flesh and pull it from her, and as it comes off you must take it from my mouth and throw it off, saying, Be a fox, a bird, or anything else, and it will then run off never to return.' When the witch begged for mercy the Great Head said, 'You had no mercy; see the dry bones; you must die,' and they killed her, and her flesh was turned into animals, and birds, and fish. Burning her to ashes, they searched for the year-old bones and laid them in rows, and when the storm and terrific hurricane arose the Great Head out of the wind called to the nine brothers to awake, and they all arose to life, shouting for joy at seeing each other and their youngest brother again.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Stone Giantess Who Nursed the Chief's Child
title.zh: 哺乳酋長之子的石巨人婦

region.en: Hunting wigwam in the olden Seneca country
region.zh: 古時塞內卡之地的獵屋

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The Stone Giant's wife'

summary.en: A stone giant woman fleeing her murderous husband enters the hunter's lodge while his wife is out, and nurses the chief's child. She warns that her food must be cooked until no blood can be tasted, or she might kill and eat them all; she hauls game a load of four men, then announces her husband is coming and directs the blows - arms, then the back of the neck - that kill him. When the family returns to the settlement she goes home to her people, needing to fear nothing.
summary.zh: 一位逃離殺夫的石巨人婦乘獵人之妻外出時入屋，為酋長的孩子哺乳。她警告她的食物必須煮到嚐不出血味，否則她或將殺而食之；她拖回四人抬不動的獵物，又預告其夫將至，指點擊殺之處——先臂後頸。一家人返村之後，她亦安然歸返族人。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. A rare domesticated Stone Giant; cannibal risk managed by cooking, a food-taboo charter.

passages.text: A great hunter set forth upon a hunting excursion and took his wife with him; he found so much game that he built a wigwam and settled down. When she returned one evening, laden with game, she was surprised at hearing a woman's voice, and as she entered her surprise changed to fear, for she saw a stone giant woman nursing the chief's child. 'Do not be afraid,' said the giantess; 'come in.' She had run away from her cruel husband, who wanted to kill her, and had come from very far, from the land of the Stone Giants. They must be careful what food they gave her: she could not eat raw food, but it must be well cooked, so thoroughly cooked that she could not taste the blood - for if she once tasted blood she might wish to kill them and the child and eat them. She knew where to find the game and would fetch it instead.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: After a while she returned bringing in one hand a load which four ordinary men could not have carried. She told her secret: 'My husband is after me. In three days he will be here. We shall have a terrible fight when he comes, and you and your husband must help me to kill him.' When he came in sight she seized him and threw him on the ground: 'Now strike him on the arms, now on the back of the neck' - and so he was finally killed, and she took him out and buried him. She staid quietly with the hunter and his wife until they were ready to leave for the settlement, then said, 'Now I must go home to my people, for I need fear nothing,' and bade them farewell.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: The Stone Giant's Challenge and the Human Finger Charm
title.zh: 石巨人的挑戰與人指法器

region.en: Rocky race-course in the Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的岩石賽道

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'The Stone Giant's challenge'

summary.en: A Stone Giant challenges a Seneca chief to a race. Leading over cornfields, bushes and brooks until his moccasins are nearly worn off, the hunter climbs rocks where the giant - who cannot raise his head - loses him, and takes a human finger from his pocket: placed upright on his hand it points the way. The hunter snatches the charm, and the giant weeps: 'You have taken my charm, and now you can always find game and all you want, for the finger will direct you to it.'
summary.zh: 石巨人向塞內卡首領下了賽跑戰書。獵人穿玉米田、灌木與溪流，鹿皮鞋幾乎磨穿，最後攀上岩石——巨人不能抬頭，迷失了他的蹤影，便自囊中取出一根人指：直豎於掌上，立即指出方向。獵人奪下法器，巨人哭道：「你奪了我的法器，如今你永遠能尋得獵物與所需，因為這手指會指引你。」

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Same finger-charm motif as Parker's 'Animated Finger' tale.

passages.text: A Stone Giant challenged a Seneca chief to a race. The challenge was accepted, and the time for the start appointed two days later. The hunter employed the time in making a pair of moccasins, and in due time the race began. The hunter was in advance; he led the way over cornfields and through bushes, over and around brooks, and went a weary distance until he was very tired and his moccasins were nearly worn off his feet. At last he began to climb rocks. Now, the Stone Giant had no power to raise his head and could not tell where the hunter was when once he was above him, and in this dilemma he had recourse to a charm, and took from his pocket a human finger. He placed it upright upon his hand, and it immediately pointed the way for him to go.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

passages.text: Now, the hunter had turned and seen him do it, so he stooped and snatched the charm from him, whereupon the giant commenced crying and said: 'You have won. You have taken my charm, and now you can always find game and all you want, for the finger will direct you to it.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.

title.en: Hiawatha and the Origin of Iroquois Wampum

region.en: Lake on the Mohawk mission road, New York (symbolic pin near the Mohawk River)
region.zh: 莫霍克傳道路上的湖（象徵性定位於莫霍克河附近）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. I: 'Hiawatha and the Iroquois wampum'

summary.en: On a mission into Mohawk country Hiawatha comes upon the borders of a lake; the whole sky fills with wild ducks which alight, quench their thirst and soak their plumage, then rise in one great mass - and the lake has become dry, its bed filled with shells. From these the wise chief proceeds to make the wampum which afterwards so firmly cemented the union of the six tribes, forming the great Iroquois Confederacy.
summary.zh: 海華沙行至莫霍克之地的湖畔；滿天野鴨落於水面，飲水解渴、浸潤羽毛，而後一齊沖天而起——湖水已乾，湖底盡是貝殼。這位睿智的酋長與謀士便以之製成貝珠，其後牢牢凝聚六族之盟，成為偉大的易洛魁聯盟。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Smith notes the wampum-name etymology is the tribe's own interpretation.

passages.text: In one of his missions into the country of the Mohawks, Hiawatha once came upon the borders of a lake. While deliberating in what manner he should cross it, the whole sky became filled with wild ducks, all of which finally alighted upon the surface of the water. After quenching their thirst and soaking their plumage they ascended again into the air in one great mass, and lo! the lake had become dry, while its bed was filled with shells. From these the wise chief and counselor proceeded to make the wampum which afterward so firmly cemented the union of the six tribes, thereby forming the great Iroquois Confederacy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. I; public domain.
